concepts.title: C++17 Value Categories: lvalue, prvalue, xvalue
concepts.content: C++17 defines expressions by identity (glvalue) and movability (rvalue). An lvalue has identity and cannot be moved from; an xvalue has identity and can be moved from; a prvalue has no identity and initializes objects directly without temporary materialization until required. Misusing std::move on a return value inhibits guaranteed copy elision by turning a prvalue into an xvalue.
concepts.image_prompt: Venn-style tree diagram with root Expression splitting into glvalue and rvalue, intersecting at xvalue, with leaf nodes lvalue, xvalue, and prvalue showing identity and movability arrows.

concepts.title: Guaranteed Copy Elision and RVO (C++17)
concepts.content: Since C++17, prvalues are not materialized until needed, guaranteeing zero-copy construction when returning a temporary of the same type (URVO), even if copy/move constructors are deleted. Named Return Value Optimization (NRVO) applies to named local variables and remains an optional compiler optimization that fails if multiple return paths return different named objects or if std::move wraps the return.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram comparing C++17 prvalue direct initialization into caller stack slot versus NRVO conditional elision on a named local object.

concepts.title: Reference Collapsing and Forwarding References
concepts.content: A forwarding reference T&& occurs only when T is a deduced template parameter or auto&&. When bound to an lvalue of type U, T deduces to U&, and reference collapsing rules fold T&& into U& (an lvalue reference falls out whenever either reference is an lvalue reference; only && + && yields &&). Qualifying as const T&& disables forwarding semantics.
concepts.image_prompt: 2x2 matrix diagram mapping Template Parameter T& and T&& against Argument Type U& and U&& with arrows converging to collapsed types U&, U&, U&, and U&&.

concepts.title: std::move vs std::forward Mechanics
concepts.content: Neither std::move nor std::forward generates runtime machine code or moves bytes; both are compile-time static_cast wrappers. std::move unconditionally casts its argument to remove_reference_t<T>&&, enabling move construction. std::forward<T> conditionally casts to T&& only when T was deduced as an rvalue (non-reference), preserving lvalue-ness for lvalue arguments in template wrappers. Calling std::move twice on the same variable reads from a moved-from object.
concepts.image_prompt: Flowchart branching from Input Expression through std::move unconditional rvalue cast versus std::forward<T> conditional branch into lvalue copy or rvalue move.

concepts.title: Move Constructors and noexcept Guarantees
concepts.content: Standard containers like std::vector preserve the strong exception guarantee during reallocation via std::move_if_noexcept. When capacity doubles, std::vector moves elements into the new buffer only if the element's move constructor is marked noexcept (or if copy construction is deleted); otherwise it falls back to copying every element. Always declare move constructors and move assignment operators noexcept unless they genuinely allocate.
concepts.image_prompt: Decision tree from std::vector::push_back reallocation checking is_nothrow_move_constructible<T> branching to Fast O(1) Pointer Steal or Slow Deep Copy Fallback.

concepts.title: Rule of Zero vs Rule of Five
concepts.content: Classes that manage business logic should follow the Rule of Zero: define no custom destructor, copy, or move operations, delegating ownership to RAII members like std::unique_ptr or std::vector. Classes managing raw resources must follow the Rule of Five: declaring even an empty ~T() suppresses implicit move generation, silently degrading moves into expensive copies unless move operations are explicitly defaulted or implemented.
concepts.image_prompt: Table diagram showing user-declared destructor suppressing implicit move constructor and move assignment while leaving copy operations deprecated.

concepts.title: Object Lifetime, Storage Duration, and Placement New
concepts.content: Storage allocation and object lifetime are decoupled in C++. Calling operator new(size) allocates raw bytes without starting lifetime; placement new — new (ptr) T(args) — constructs the object in pre-allocated aligned storage and begins its lifetime. When using custom arenas, you must explicitly invoke std::destroy_at(p) (or p->~T()) before freeing the underlying storage buffer, never delete ptr.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline bar showing Raw Storage Allocation, Placement New starting Object Lifetime, Active Use, std::destroy_at ending Lifetime, and Storage Deallocation.

concepts.title: Implicit-Lifetime Types and std::start_lifetime_as (C++23)
concepts.content: Reading network packets or mmap buffers by casting char* to a struct pointer violates object lifetime rules unless an object actually exists at that address. C++20 introduced implicit-lifetime types (trivially constructible aggregates/scalars), and C++23 added std::start_lifetime_as<T>(void* p), which implicitly creates an object of implicit-lifetime type T over existing bytes without running initialization code or zeroing memory.
concepts.image_prompt: Block diagram showing Raw Byte Buffer passing through std::start_lifetime_as<Header> node to produce a valid typed Header* pointer without modifying underlying bytes.

concepts.title: Strict Aliasing Rule and std::bit_cast (C++20)
concepts.content: Accessing an object of type T through a glvalue of an unrelated type U (e.g., *(uint32_t*)&my_float) is undefined behavior under the strict aliasing rule, allowing compilers to reorder loads and stores across both pointers. Only char, unsigned char, and std::byte may alias any type. Use C++20 std::bit_cast<To>(from) or std::memcpy for zero-overhead, type-safe bit reinterpretation.
concepts.image_prompt: Split comparison diagram showing Undefined Behavior reinterpret_cast<uint32_t*>(float*) crossed out versus valid constexpr std::bit_cast<uint32_t>(float) register transfer.

concepts.title: Pointer Provenance and std::launder (C++17)
concepts.content: When you placement-new a new object over storage previously occupied by an object with const or reference members or a different dynamic type, the original pointer retains provenance to the old object, letting the compiler hoist invariant reads. Calling std::launder(p) acts as an optimization barrier that returns a pointer bound to the newly constructed object at the same address.
concepts.image_prompt: Memory slot diagram showing Old Object with const member replaced via Placement New, with Old Pointer blocked and std::launder(p) routing to New Object.

concepts.title: Struct Alignment, Padding, and alignas / alignof
concepts.content: Every type has an alignment requirement queried via alignof(T), and structs are padded so each member sits at an offset divisible by its alignment, with total sizeof(T) rounded to the largest member alignment. Ordering struct members from largest to smallest alignment eliminates internal padding holes. Over-aligning a type via alignas(64) prevents false sharing and triggers aligned operator new(size_t, std::align_val_t) in C++17.
concepts.image_prompt: Memory layout comparison of poorly ordered 24-byte struct with 3 padding gaps versus size-sorted 16-byte struct packed into two 8-byte words.

concepts.title: Empty Base Optimization and [[no_unique_address]] (C++20)
concepts.content: Every distinct C++ object requires sizeof >= 1 so two objects have unique addresses, meaning an empty stateless allocator or comparator member adds 1–8 bytes of padding to a class. Before C++20, libraries inherited privately from empty types to trigger Empty Base Optimization (EBO). In C++20, marking a data member [[no_unique_address]] allows it to overlap with subsequent members or tail padding.
concepts.image_prompt: Struct memory map comparing 16-byte class with 1-byte StatelessDeleter plus 7-byte padding against 8-byte class using [[no_unique_address]] overlapping address space.

concepts.title: Virtual Tables (vtable), vptr Layout, and Devirtualization
concepts.content: A class with virtual functions adds one hidden vptr (8 bytes on 64-bit targets) per polymorphic base subobject, pointing to a read-only vtable of function pointers and RTTI metadata. Virtual dispatch costs an extra pointer dereference and blocks inlining. Marking leaf classes or methods final lets the compiler devirtualize calls at compile time and inline the target function directly.
concepts.image_prompt: Pointer diagram from Stack/Heap Object containing vptr and fields pointing to .rodata vtable array indexing into Target Virtual Function code.

concepts.title: std::unique_ptr Custom Deleters and Zero-Overhead Sizing
concepts.content: std::unique_ptr<T, D> enforces exclusive ownership with zero size overhead over a raw pointer (sizeof == 8 bytes) when D is a stateless functor or stateless captureless lambda (C++20), leveraging EBO or [[no_unique_address]]. Using a function pointer std::unique_ptr<FILE, int(*)(FILE*)> swells the smart pointer to 16 bytes, and using std::function<void(T*)> swells it to 40–64 bytes.
concepts.image_prompt: Bar comparison diagram showing sizeof(unique_ptr) at 8 bytes with Stateless Struct Deleter, 16 bytes with Function Pointer, and 40 bytes with std::function.

concepts.title: std::shared_ptr Control Block and std::make_shared Trade-offs
concepts.content: A std::shared_ptr is 16 bytes: one pointer to T and one pointer to a thread-safe heap Control Block storing strong count, weak count, and deleter. Constructing via std::shared_ptr<T>(new T) performs two heap allocations, whereas std::make_shared<T>() fuses the control block and T into one contiguous allocation. Trade-off: make_shared cannot release T's memory until all std::weak_ptr instances also expire.
concepts.image_prompt: Dual heap layout comparing separate Object and Control Block allocations versus std::make_shared single fused block held alive by a lingering weak_ptr.

concepts.title: std::shared_ptr Aliasing Constructor and enable_shared_from_this
concepts.content: The aliasing constructor shared_ptr<U>(const shared_ptr<T>& owner, U* member) shares reference counts with owner while pointing directly to a subobject or interior buffer member. To safely create a shared_ptr from this inside a method without allocating a duplicate control block (causing double free), inherit publicly from std::enable_shared_from_this<T> and call shared_from_this() only after a shared_ptr already owns the instance.
concepts.image_prompt: Object graph showing Aliasing shared_ptr pointing to interior Member field while sharing Control Block reference count with outer Owner shared_ptr.

concepts.title: Small Buffer Optimization (SBO / SSO) and Move Costs
concepts.content: Types like std::string (typically 15–22 bytes inline capacity on 64-bit libc++/libstdc++) and std::function (typically 16–24 bytes inline) store small payloads directly inside the object's stack footprint to avoid heap allocation. Consequence: moving an SSO string or SBO std::function is O(N) bytes copied rather than an O(1) pointer swap, and capturing large lambdas in std::function silently triggers heap allocation.
concepts.image_prompt: Union layout diagram of 24-byte std::string showing Short Mode with 22 inline chars versus Long Mode with heap pointer, size, and capacity.

concepts.title: Non-Owning Views: std::string_view (C++17) and std::span (C++20)
concepts.content: std::string_view (const char* + size_t) and std::span<T, Extent> (T* + size_t, or just T* when Extent is fixed at compile time) provide cheap, pass-by-value bounds-aware views over contiguous memory without allocation or copying. Warning: string_view::data() is NOT guaranteed to be null-terminated after substr() or prefix trimming, and returning a view to a function-local container creates an immediate dangling pointer.
concepts.image_prompt: Pointer diagram showing 16-byte std::string_view (ptr, len) referencing a slice inside a larger buffer with no trailing null terminator.

concepts.title: Iterator and Reference Invalidation Rules in STL Containers
concepts.content: Adding elements to std::vector invalidates all pointers, references, and iterators whenever size() exceeds capacity(), whereas std::deque invalidates all iterators on push_front/push_back but preserves element references. Node-based containers (std::list, std::map) never invalidate references on insertion. Flat hash tables (std::unordered_map) invalidate all iterators when load_factor() exceeds max_load_factor() and triggers a rehash, though node references remain valid.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison diagram showing std::vector reallocation invalidating old buffer pointers versus std::deque chunk array growth preserving element addresses.

concepts.title: Polymorphic Memory Resources (std::pmr) and Arena Allocators (C++17)
concepts.content: Standard std::vector<T, CustomAlloc> bakes the allocator into the type signature. <memory_resource> decouples allocation strategy via std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>, which holds a pointer to a virtual std::pmr::memory_resource. Pairing std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource backed by a stack array with pmr::vector bumps a pointer for O(1) allocations and no-op individual deallocations, releasing all memory at once when the arena goes out of scope.
concepts.image_prompt: Architecture diagram showing pmr::vector delegating through polymorphic_allocator to monotonic_buffer_resource backed by a stack std::byte[4096] buffer with bump pointer.

concepts.title: Arena & Pool Allocators: Fragmentation and Lifetime Coupling
concepts.content: General-purpose allocators (ptmalloc, jemalloc, mimalloc) incur metadata overhead, lock/thread-cache contention, and external fragmentation under high-churn workloads. std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource groups allocations into size-classed slab pools for single-threaded O(1) reuse without atomic instructions. Crucial failure mode: a pmr container stores a raw pointer to its memory_resource, so the resource must strictly outlive all containers using it.
concepts.image_prompt: Slab pool diagram showing unsynchronized_pool_resource dispatching 32-byte, 64-byte, and 128-byte size class free-lists to local containers.

concepts.title: C++11 Memory Model: Sequenced-Before, Happens-Before, and Data Races
concepts.content: In C++, a data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and neither access is atomic or ordered by happens-before. Any data race causes complete Undefined Behavior—not merely torn reads. A happens-before edge is formed either within a thread via sequenced-before or across threads via synchronizes-with on atomic or mutex operations.
concepts.image_prompt: Two-thread timeline showing Thread 1 non-atomic write and Thread 2 read lacking a synchronizes-with edge resulting in Data Race Undefined Behavior.

concepts.title: std::atomic, Lock-Free Guarantees, and Torn Reads/Writes
concepts.content: std::atomic<T> guarantees indivisible loads, stores, and read-modify-write (RMW) operations for trivially copyable types T. However, std::atomic<BigStruct> may silently use an internal spinlock pool if sizeof(T) exceeds hardware atomic width (typically 8 or 16 bytes on x86-64/ARM64). Always assert std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free at compile time in real-time, signal-handler, or shared-memory code.
concepts.image_prompt: Decision flow from std::atomic<T> checking sizeof(T) <= 16 bytes and alignment to select Lock-Free CPU instruction (LOCK CMPXCHG16B) versus internal Mutex Table.

concepts.title: Acquire-Release Ordering vs Sequential Consistency (seq_cst)
concepts.content: The default memory_order_seq_cst enforces a single total global modification order across all threads, emitting a costly MFENCE or LOCK XCHG on x86 stores and full barriers on ARM64. Pairing store(val, memory_order_release) in a producer with load(memory_order_acquire) in a consumer establishes a synchronizes-with edge: all memory writes before the release store become visible after the acquire load, compiling to plain MOVs on x86-64 and LDAR/STLR on ARM64.
concepts.image_prompt: Two-thread message passing diagram showing Thread A payload writes before store(release) synchronizing with Thread B load(acquire) before payload reads.

concepts.title: memory_order_relaxed and Reference Counting Semantics
concepts.content: memory_order_relaxed guarantees atomicity and modification-order consistency for a single atomic variable, with zero ordering constraints or compiler barriers on surrounding memory accesses. In std::shared_ptr, incrementing the strong reference count uses fetch_add(1, memory_order_relaxed) because holding an existing reference already proves the object is alive; however, decrementing MUST use fetch_sub(1, memory_order_acq_rel) so prior mutations happen-before the destructor runs on the last thread.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline of shared_ptr lifecycle showing fetch_add(relaxed) on copy versus fetch_sub(acq_rel) on destruction synchronizing prior thread writes before delete.

concepts.title: Compare-And-Swap (CAS) Loops and the ABA Problem
concepts.content: Lock-free algorithms update state via compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired) inside a retry loop (use weak in loops to avoid extra branches on LL/SC architectures like ARM64 where spurious failures occur). The ABA problem happens when Thread 1 reads pointer A, gets preempted while Thread 2 frees A, allocates a new node at the same address A, and pushes it back—causing Thread 1's CAS to succeed on corrupted state. Mitigate with 128-bit tagged pointers (aba_tag + ptr) or hazard pointers (C++26).
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram of Lock-Free Stack showing Thread 1 reading Top=A, Thread 2 popping A and B then pushing recycled A, and Thread 1 CAS falsely succeeding.

concepts.title: CPU Cache Hierarchy, Cache Lines, and Hardware Prefetching
concepts.content: Modern CPUs transfer memory between RAM (~60–100 ns latency) and L1 cache (~1 ns latency) in fixed 64-byte cache lines (128 bytes on Apple Silicon M-series). Hardware stream prefetchers detect sequential stride accesses in contiguous std::vector buffers and preload upcoming cache lines into L1/L2 automatically. Pointer-chasing structures like std::list or tree nodes scatter allocations across heap pages, causing L3 cache misses and TLB thrashing on every hop.
concepts.image_prompt: Memory hierarchy diagram showing CPU Core -> L1 (1ns) -> L2 (4ns) -> L3 (15ns) -> DRAM (80ns) transferring 64-byte cache lines sequentially versus scattered pointer hops.

concepts.title: False Sharing and std::hardware_destructive_interference_size
concepts.content: When two threads concurrently modify independent variables (e.g., per-thread counters in an array) that reside on the same 64-byte cache line, the MESI cache coherency protocol repeatedly invalidates and bounces the entire cache line between CPU cores, degrading throughput by 10x–50x. Prevent false sharing by aligning independent hot fields with alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size) (or alignas(64) when ABI stability across targets is required).
concepts.image_prompt: Dual-core cache diagram showing Core 0 writing Counter[0] and Core 1 writing Counter[1] on the same 64-byte cache line causing MESI invalidation ping-pong, solved by alignas(64) separation.

concepts.title: Data-Oriented Design: AoS vs SoA Memory Layouts
concepts.content: An Array of Structs (AoS, e.g., std::vector<Particle> with x, y, z, color, name, metadata) loads cold fields into every 64-byte cache line even when a hot loop only updates position. Refactoring into a Struct of Arrays (SoA) with contiguous float x[], y[], z[] arrays packs 16 floats per 64-byte cache line, achieves 100% cache line utilization, and allows automatic AVX2/AVX-512 SIMD vectorization.
concepts.image_prompt: Cache line layout comparing AoS packing 1 Particle (hot xyz + cold metadata) per 64-byte line versus SoA packing 16 contiguous hot x floats for SIMD load.

concepts.title: Compile-Time Evaluation: constexpr, consteval, and constinit (C++20)
concepts.content: constexpr functions can execute at either compile time or runtime, and since C++20 support virtual calls, try/catch, and transient heap allocations via new/delete inside constant expressions. consteval (immediate functions) forces every call to produce a compile-time constant or fail compilation. constinit guarantees a static or thread_local variable is initialized at compile time—eliminating the Static Initialization Order Fiasco—while keeping the variable mutable at runtime.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison matrix mapping constexpr, consteval, and constinit across Compile-Time Evaluation Required, Runtime Execution Allowed, and Runtime Mutability.

concepts.title: C++20 Concepts and Requires Clauses vs SFINAE
concepts.content: C++20 Concepts replace unreadable std::enable_if_t SFINAE templates with named compile-time boolean predicates evaluated via requires clauses. Concepts participate in partial ordering via constraint subsumption: an overload constrained by std::random_access_iterator automatically wins over std::forward_iterator without ambiguous call errors because its atomic constraints subsume the weaker concept. Prefer standard <concepts> before writing ad-hoc requires(T x) expressions.
concepts.image_prompt: Concept hierarchy diagram showing random_access_iterator subsuming bidirectional_iterator and forward_iterator during overload resolution.

concepts.title: Type Erasure Internals: Virtual Dispatch vs Function-Pointer Tables
concepts.content: Type erasure (used by std::function and std::any) decouples an interface from concrete template types without requiring a shared base class. Internally, a wrapper holds a Small Buffer Optimization (SBO) storage union plus either a pointer to an abstract Concept base class implemented by a templated Model<T> derived class, or a static vtable struct of function pointers (invoke, destroy, clone/move) to eliminate an extra vptr indirection.
concepts.image_prompt: Internal architecture of Type-Erased Wrapper showing 24-byte SBO Storage Buffer alongside a Static Function Table pointer dispatching invoke, move, and destroy.

concepts.title: CRTP vs C++23 Deducing This (Explicit Object Parameters)
concepts.content: The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (class Derived : public Base<Derived>) achieves static polymorphism and mixin composition without virtual dispatch by static_casting this to Derived*. However, CRTP requires boilerplate helper casts and fails cleanly with deep inheritance chains. C++23 Deducing This allows declaring void foo(this Self&& self), deducing the exact derived type and value category (const/&/&&) in a single non-virtual template method.
concepts.image_prompt: Side-by-side class diagram comparing CRTP Base<Derived> static_cast<Derived*>(this) pattern against C++23 explicit object parameter (this Self&& self).

concepts.title: C++20 Stackless Coroutines: Promise, Handle, and Frame Allocation
concepts.content: A C++20 coroutine is a function containing co_await, co_yield, or co_return. By default, the compiler allocates a coroutine frame on the heap (via operator new) holding parameters, local variables across suspension points, and the promise_type object. Heap allocation Removal Optimization (HALO) elides this heap allocation and embeds the frame in the caller's stack only when the coroutine's lifetime is provably nested within the caller and inlined.
concepts.image_prompt: Memory diagram showing Caller holding lightweight std::coroutine_handle<> pointing to a Heap Coroutine Frame containing Promise, Saved Registers, and Local State.

concepts.title: Structured Concurrency: std::jthread and Cooperative Stop Tokens (C++20)
concepts.content: Unlike std::thread, which calls std::terminate() if destroyed while joinable(), C++20 std::jthread automatically calls request_stop() and join() in its destructor. It pairs with std::stop_source and std::stop_token for thread-safe cooperative cancellation, and std::stop_callback registers an RAII callback (such as waking a condition_variable_any or canceling an I/O operation) that fires immediately if stop is already requested.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram showing std::jthread destructor invoking request_stop() on shared Stop State, triggering std::stop_callback and waking Worker Thread before join().

concepts.title: Modern Synchronization Primitives: std::latch, std::barrier, and Atomic Wait (C++20)
concepts.content: Avoid spinlocks and heavyweight mutex+condition_variable pairs for simple thread coordination. std::latch is a single-use downward atomic counter for fork-join initialization, while std::barrier is a reusable phase counter that executes a noexcept completion function before releasing waiting threads. On individual variables, std::atomic::wait(old) and notify_one() map directly to OS futex syscalls (FUTEX_WAIT / WaitOnAddress) with zero extra heap or mutex size.
concepts.image_prompt: Thread barrier diagram showing 4 Worker Threads calling arrive_and_wait(), invoking the Phase Completion Function on the last arrival, then unblocking all threads for Phase 2.

concepts.title: Zero-Cost Exceptions (Itanium ABI) vs std::expected<T, E> (C++23)
concepts.content: Table-driven exceptions (Itanium C++ ABI) have near-zero runtime cost on the happy path by storing unwind instructions in side-table ELF sections (.eh_frame / .gcc_except_table), but throwing incurs microseconds of stack unwinding, dynamic RTTI matching, and global dl_iterate_phdr locks under contention. Use C++23 std::expected<T, E> (a discriminated union with monadic and_then / transform) for recoverable, high-frequency errors or latency-critical paths.
concepts.image_prompt: Dual path diagram contrasting Normal Return via CPU registers (std::expected<T,E>) against Exception Throw traversing .eh_frame DWARF unwind tables.

concepts.title: std::variant Visitation and Overloaded Lambda Dispatch (C++17)
concepts.content: std::variant<Ts...> is a type-safe, stack-allocated tagged union that never allocates on the heap (unlike boost::variant backup heap), guaranteeing zero dynamic memory overhead at the cost of a rare valueless_by_exception state if a throwing type assignment fails. Combine std::visit with the C++17 deduction guide pattern template<class... Ts> struct overloaded : Ts... { using Ts::operator()...; }; for jump-table-compiled pattern matching.
concepts.image_prompt: Memory layout of std::variant<int, double, string> showing aligned union storage plus 1-byte type index dispatching through std::visit jump table.

concepts.title: Undefined Behavior (UB) and Compiler Optimization Exploits
concepts.content: In C++, compilers assume Undefined Behavior (signed integer overflow, null pointer dereference, uninitialized scalar reads, shifting by >= bit-width, or infinite loops without side effects/atomics) never happens. A null check if (p == nullptr) placed AFTER an earlier *p dereference will be completely deleted by dead-code elimination at -O2. Compile with -fno-strict-aliasing or -fwrapv only as legacy mitigations; fix UB at the source.
concepts.image_prompt: Compiler pipeline diagram showing Source Code with *p before if (!p) entering LLVM Optimizer at -O2 and outputting assembly with the null check stripped.

concepts.title: Runtime Verification: ASan, TSan, UBSan, and Valgrind
concepts.content: Memory bugs in C++ require instrumentation sanitizers in CI. AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) uses shadow memory (1 byte per 8 bytes of RAM) and redzones to catch use-after-free, heap/stack buffer overflows, and use-after-return with ~2x slowdown (vs ~20x for Valgrind). ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread) tracks vector clocks per memory access to detect data races and lock-order inversions without requiring the race to manifest as a crash.
concepts.image_prompt: Shadow memory mapping diagram showing 8-byte Application Heap Slot and Poisoned Redzones mapped to 1-byte ASan Shadow Memory catching an out-of-bounds read.
